chapter: Stuff Smith stories, Wes Montgomery and singers
title: Strings standing for Sarah; Ella Fitzgerald plays piano and harmonica
summary: String players stood for Sarah Vaughan after one take; Ella surprised Jones playing piano and harmonica she learned for her union card.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: And they just -- the only other time I saw that happen, we did a -- I had a big string date, a big orchestra date with Sarah Vaughan, and I was conducting, and Sarah would come in, and on one take in the studio -- we'd go in and rehearse and get the balance of it first, you know?
Uh-huh.

Get everything laid out, and so she'd just walk in and sing it one time, and that was it. And the string section would stand up. I'd never seen that with a singer in a studio. Now, the other experience I had had was with Ella Fitzgerald. She was the only one I knew that would just travel around the world and there were standing ovations. Everywhere she went, you know?
How about Sarah -- I mean Sarah is about the only singer you worked with who was also a musician too,
isn't she? I mean like Ella's certainly a very musical singer, but Ella isn't a musician, as Sarah is, is she?
Well, Ella surprised me one day, over at her house.
How?
Playing piano.
Oh, really?
And harmonica.
Harmonica?
Yeah. She said she had to do that to get her 802 card in the union.
Oh.
You know, it surprised the heck out of me but she -- you would never know it, you know.
But everybody knows Sarah plays piano.
Yeah.
I didn't know that Ella did.

Uh-huh. She played like a pretty stiff tune, 'Stomping At the Savoy.' I said, 'Fitz, those are some pretty rough changes in the channel,' and she said, 'Well, that's the only way I could get my 802 card.'
(Laughter)
So Edgar Samson taught it to her.
I'll be darned.
